page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: What it is
lines: 393 K to make plaster of Paris.
If gypsum is heated above 393 K, all
This anhydrous CaSO₄ is dead burnt
steps.why: Dead burnt plaster is defined by the temperature. Up to 393 K the solid keeps half a water molecule and is plaster of Paris; above 393 K it keeps none, and the product is the anhydrous salt.
common_mistakes: Writing that dead burnt plaster still holds half a water molecule. It holds none, so it is anhydrous CaSO₄.
Writing the temperature as 393 °C. The figure is 393 K.
steps.memory_tip: Above 393 K the last of the water leaves and only CaSO₄ is left.
steps.margin_note: Write the temperature 393 K beside the equation.

steps.label: Why it is called dead burnt

with water, because it does not take
the water back to form gypsum.
A plaster that has lost this setting
plaster, and it cannot be used as a
steps.why: The name records the loss of the one property that makes plaster useful. Overheating removes the setting action, so the material is of no use as a plaster even though it is still calcium sulphate.
common_mistakes: Writing that dead burnt plaster sets slowly. It has lost its setting property; mixing it with water does not give a hard mass.
Naming the product without saying why it is called dead. The lost setting property is the reason.
steps.memory_tip: Dead means it no longer sets with water.
steps.margin_note: State the temperature limit and the lost setting property together.

insider_note: A complete answer names the temperature limit of 393 K and says that the anhydrous product no longer sets with water.
